name: SSHash
workload: Exact membership/lookup queries over billions of DNA k-mers (human and bacterial pangenome datasets) using an MPHF (PTHash) plus minimizer-based bucketing, benchmarked single-threaded.
claimed_speedup: 990 ns/k-mer positive lookup, 854 ns/k-mer negative lookup on the human dataset (canonical SSHash); 9.39 bits/k-mer space; 16.2 min / 17.3 GB peak memory to construct on the human dataset (derived from page data: paper Tables 4/5/7)
hardware: Intel Core i9-9940X (single core used for benchmarks), Ubuntu 19.10, Linux kernel 5.3.0, 64-bit
tradeoffs: Specialized to fixed-length DNA k-mer keys (not a general-purpose MPHF library); static/immutable once built; relies on PTHash internally so inherits its construction-time/space tradeoffs; needs minimizer sampling tuned per dataset.
caveats: Comparison is against domain-specific k-mer dictionaries (Pufferfish, BLight, dBG-FM), not against std::unordered_map, CMPH, or BBHash directly, so it is only indirect evidence for the MPHF category baseline; numbers are from the peer-reviewed paper (Bioinformatics 2022), not a blog per se, but was surfaced via a k-mer/MPHF blog roundup.
found_via: Blogs / talks: Camille Marchet's 'Minimal Perfect Hash Functions in the k-mer world' blog post (https://kamimrcht.github.io/webpage/mphf.html), which links to SSHash as a genomics MPHF-based dictionary; verified against the SSHash paper and GitHub repo.

name: BLight
workload: Exact associative index over k-mers of the human genome (k=31): build the index and answer membership/identifier queries over the full reference, using an MPHF (BBHash-style) plus minimizer indexing.
claimed_speedup: Human genome (k=31): 10 min construction / 7.4 GB peak memory / 22.3 bits/k-mer for BLight vs 69 min / 27.4 GB / 55.59 bits/k-mer for Pufferfish; full-reference query time 1,748s single-thread (155s at 12 threads) vs Pufferfish 1,799s single-thread (verbatim from paper Tables 1-2)
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2420 @ 1.90 GHz, 192 GB RAM, Ubuntu 16.04
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 is copyleft and network-use-triggering, a stronger restriction than most catalog entries; specialized to k-mer/genomics keys; static index (no updates) as opposed to Bifrost's dynamic index.
caveats: Compiler/build flags not stated in the paper text I could confirm, so capped at Tier B; only compared against Pufferfish, not std::unordered_map/BBHash/CMPH directly; repo last pushed mid-2024 (stale).
found_via: Blogs / talks: surfaced from the same k-mer/MPHF blog roundup (kamimrcht.github.io/webpage/mphf.html) and cross-checked against the BLight Bioinformatics paper and GitHub repo.

name: RSHash
workload: Streaming and single k-mer lookup/build over large k-mer sets (genome datasets from Pibiri 2022), comparing a rank/select-bitvector hash construction against SSHash's PTHash-based dictionary.
claimed_speedup: RSHash is on average 1.4x and up to 2x faster than SSHash5 in streaming lookups (4.5x more k-mers/sec on average, up to 8.5x vs published SSHash3); ~0.5 microsecond/k-mer single lookup (fast variant), ~0.6 microsecond/k-mer (compact variant); 50% faster negative lookups; built 60% faster than SSHash using 40% less memory (verbatim from paper)
hardware: AMD EPYC 9454 @ 2.75 GHz, 1 TB RAM, single core, Debian (kernel 6.1.0-43), 64-bit
tradeoffs: Uses succinct rank/select bitvectors rather than a classical MPHF construction, so it is a competing technique in the same k-mer-dictionary space rather than an MPHF library itself; specialized to DNA k-mers, not general-purpose keys; very new/low-adoption project.
caveats: Baseline is another k-mer dictionary (SSHash) rather than std::unordered_map/CMPH/BBHash directly, so this is indirect (comparative) evidence for the category, included per orchestrator's genomics-blog guidance; project is very new (created Feb 2026) with only 8 stars.
found_via: Blogs / talks: found while following the k-mer MPHF blog trail from Camille Marchet's page and the SSHash lineage of papers; confirmed via the peer-reviewed RSHash paper (Bioinformatics 2026) and its GitHub repo/README.

name: PtrHash (author benchmark blog)
workload: Query throughput and construction time for a minimal perfect hash function over 300 million string keys and 10^9 integer keys, single machine, multi-threaded construction.
claimed_speedup: PtrHash Fast: 33 ns/query (loop), 16 ns/query (streaming), 27 ns/key construction (6 threads), 2.99 bits/key; PtrHash Default: 37/23 ns/query, 32 ns/key construction, 2.40 bits/key; vs PTHash-CC 77 ns/query and PHOBIC 108-179 ns/query; ~8 ns/key streaming query on 10^9 integer keys, 'just short of the 7.4 ns inverse throughput of random memory access' (verbatim from author's blog)
hardware: Intel Core i7-10750H, 6 cores, 2.6 GHz, DDR4-3200
tradeoffs: Rust implementation (usable from C via FFI, not a native C++ library); numbers are self-reported by the author on their own blog, matching the companion SEA 2025 paper.
caveats: This is a first-party author blog post (not independent), and exact compiler flags for the reported numbers were not stated on the page, so capped at Tier B even though the underlying repo and a peer-reviewed paper (SEA 2025) exist. ptrhash's canonical repo is already on the KNOWN_LIST, so this is reported only as additional evidence for a known project.
found_via: Blogs / talks: web search 'minimal perfect hash function benchmark blog comparison BBHash PTHash' surfaced 'PtrHash: Minimal Perfect Hashing at RAM Throughput · CuriousCoding' (author's own engineering blog), opened and verified directly.

name: Engineering Minimal/k-Perfect Hash Functions (stefanfred implementation)
workload: k-perfect hash function construction and query benchmarks including the k=1 (standard minimal perfect hashing) case, evaluated against prior MPHF/k-perfect-hash constructions on large key sets.
claimed_speedup: Paper states the four new constructions 'simultaneously dominate older approaches in space consumption, construction time, and query time,' with query times in the single-digit nanoseconds per key range for the k=1 case, compared explicitly against BBHash, PTHash, RecSplit, and CHD; exact table values are embedded as images in the PDF and could not be extracted verbatim
tradeoffs: Very new, low-adoption research code (1 star); generalizes to k-perfect hashing (buckets may hold up to k keys), of which minimal perfect hashing is the k=1 special case; GPL-3.0 is copyleft.
caveats: Peer-reviewed at ESA 2025 (DROPS: 10.4230/LIPIcs.ESA.2025.99) and compares directly against BBHash/PTHash/RecSplit/CHD per the paper text, but the exact numeric benchmark tables are rendered as images in the PDF and hardware/compiler details could not be confirmed from the extracted text, so capped at Tier B rather than A.
found_via: Blogs / talks: web search '"Engineering Minimal k-Perfect Hash Functions" github code' following up on the Modern Minimal Perfect Hashing survey discussion; opened the arXiv paper and linked GitHub repo directly.
